The higher dose partly refutes my prediction. Under C(−3.0) the new-loop onsets do respond: Δlp = −0.180 ± 0.048, against −0.031 at C(−1.5), and above my predicted ceiling of −0.08. The persistent-loop onsets fall to −0.463, about three times the C(−1.5) effect. But ordinary novel lines now lose probability as well (−0.065 and −0.140, against about 0 at C(−1.5)). The selectivity ratio of onset to novel effect drops from very high to about 3.

So the gain does reach weak-signal loops at higher dose. The price is degrading normal reasoning steps, which plausibly explains why C(−2.25) freed no more loops in generation than C(−1.5) and gained nothing more. The submission C(−1.5) is restored and verified.

Three passes remain. One question bears directly on how to read my reported gain: how much of the per-problem flips survive a change in batching? The evaluation will batch differently, and my notes warn that separate passes do not reproduce exactly. I'll re-run the frozen submission "both" on holdout_1 in reversed order, which is a different request with a different batch layout. It is for robustness only and will not be used for selection or pooled into the gain. If most of pass 29's 24 wrong→right and 9 right→wrong flips recur, the measured gain reflects real per-problem effects. If many vanish, the SE understates the uncertainty.

This is the reproducibility pass: the frozen submission C(−1.5) against the original on holdout_1's 256 problems in reversed order. Afterwards I'll compare each problem's grade with pass 29. A high share of matching flips would mean the HOLDOUT gain reflects stable per-problem effects.

With batching reordered, C(−1.5) on holdout_1 gives +4.3 ± 2.2 (22 wrong→right, 11 right→wrong), against +5.9 ± 2.2 (24/9) in pass 29. That is the same sign at a similar size. Accuracies are 18.8% → 23.0%, against 18.4% → 24.2%.

Next I'll measure the per-problem reproducibility:
- for each model, the share of problems with the same grade in both passes, and the share with identical text;
- how many of pass 29's flips recur in pass 48.

This quantifies the batching noise the evaluation will also see.

Grades reproduce well across batching even though texts often do not. About 97–98% of problems get the same grade in both passes, while only 62–68% of texts are identical. Of pass 29's 24 wrong→right flips, 20 recur, and 7 of its 9 right→wrong flips do. The holdout_1 gain is thus mostly per-problem and stable, not batching luck. Batching alone changes about 2–3% of grades per model, which adds only a little uncertainty beyond the reported SE.

For a second, contrasting reproducibility point, I'll do the same on holdout_3, where C(−1.5) measured −0.78 (15/17). If that set's churn also recurs, the HOLDOUT variation reflects real per-problem gains and losses (fragile near-ties, as diagnosed). If it does not, much of it is batching noise. Again, this is not pooled into the gain.
